query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In a lightweight FeNiCuAl-based high-entropy alloy, introducing moderate Cr additions induces short-range atomic ordering that enhances mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance while preserving low density.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline FeNiCuAl lightweight high-entropy alloy, melt-cast and homogenized, with no chromium content and exhibiting moderate strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance.
generation.intervention: Systematically dope half of the samples with a moderate concentration of Cr (e.g., 5–10 atomic percent) while leaving the other half at zero Cr content to serve as a control.
generation.conditions: Comparatively evaluate (a) tensile and hardness properties at ambient and elevated temperatures up to ~800°C, (b) corrosion rates in salt-spray or 3.5% NaCl testing at ambient temperature, and (c) mass gain or oxide-layer evolution during exposure to air at ~900°C. Assess whether short-range ordering forms in the Cr-doped alloy using structural characterization (e.g., high-resolution TEM).
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range atomic ordering in the presence of Cr, which is hypothesized to refine the microstructure and stabilize protective Al2O3/Cr2O3 oxide scales during high-temperature exposure, while limiting bulk density increases.
generation.mechanism: Local chemical environments rich in Al and Cr enable the formation of dense oxide layers and reduce diffusion pathways, slowing corrosion and oxidation, while promoting enhanced lattice cohesion and mechanical strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the Cr-free baseline, the Cr-doped alloys will exhibit measurably higher elevated-temperature strength, substantially reduced oxide growth at 900°C, and lower corrosion current in salt-spray testing, without significantly increasing density.
generation.baseline: The undoped FeNiCuAl alloy, which lacks a strong driving force for short-range ordering or stable Al2O3/Cr2O3 oxide formation, leading to lower high-temperature oxidation resistance and somewhat lesser corrosion performance.
generation.boundary: If Cr levels exceed ~15 at.% or Al content is insufficient, the short-range ordering and oxide-layer benefits may not form or may be overshadowed by phase instability or brittleness, invalidating the hypothesis beyond that compositional range.
generation.uncertainty: Exact strength gains and oxidation rates depend on specific alloy processing and microstructure; the short-range ordering, if too strong or too weak, might reduce ductility or fail to confer a protective oxide layer.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate both undoped and Cr-doped FeNiCuAl high-entropy alloys under identical processing conditions. Verify short-range ordering via diffraction or high-resolution electron microscopy, then measure mechanical properties and perform corrosion and high-temperature oxidation testing.
measurements: Salt-spray or potentiodynamic polarization testing in NaCl solution
High-temperature oxidation weight-gain or TGA measurements (up to ~900°C)
SRO features via diffraction and local structure analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-doped alloy does not exhibit stronger mechanical properties, a denser or more protective oxide scale, or improved corrosion resistance relative to the baseline, then the short-range ordering hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), a novel class of multi-principal element alloys, brought a new era in the study of alloy materials []. The presence of five or more elements in close proximity to the iso-atomic ratio endows alloys with high configurational entropy, which confers upon HEAs the capacity to form stable simple solid solution phases. This, in turn, endows HEAs with exceptional mechanical properties and commendable corrosion resistance []. This property gives high-entropy alloys excellent mechanical and physical properties, including high strength, high fracture toughness, and the ability to conduct electricity at very low temperatures []. In addition, they exhibit excellent resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Consequently, in the aerospace field [], where the temperature of service varies widely, in the field of ultra-high temperature structural materials [], in marine industrial equipment [], and in the nuclear industry [], where there are harsh working conditions, high-entropy alloys have a wider range of application prospects than traditional alloys due to their rich elemental composition and flexible selection of elemental content. This study synthesized FeNiCuAlX high-entropy alloys (HEAs) (where X = Cr, Co, Mn) using arc melting and investigated their high-temperature oxidation behavior in air at 900 °C. The oxidation kinetics of all alloys followed a parabolic rate, with the oxidation rate constants (kp) of FeNiCuAlCr, FeNiCuAlCo, and FeNiCuAlMn being approximately two to three orders of magnitude lower than that of the FeNiCu alloy. Specifically, FeNiCuAlCr exhibited the lowest kp value of 1.72 × 10−6 mg2·cm4/s, which is significantly lower than those of FeNiCuAlCo (3.29 × 10−6 mg2·cm4/s) and FeNiCuAlMn (1.71 × 10−5 mg2·cm4/s). This suggests that the addition of chromium promotes the formation of a dense Al2O3/Cr2O3 oxide layer, significantly enhancing the oxidation resistance. Furthermore, corrosion resistance was assessed through potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy in a 3.5% NaCl solution. FeNiCuAlCr demonstrated exceptional resistance to localized corrosion, as indicated by its low corrosion current density (45.7 μA/cm2) and high pitting potential (−0.21 V), highlighting its superior corrosion performance.

chosen.lever: Elemental composition to control short-range atomic ordering
chosen.technique: Systematic doping and direct comparison to a baseline alloy under tensile, corrosion, and oxidation tests
chosen.conditions: Elevated temperature (up to ~800–900°C) in air or oxidizing atmospheres, plus standard aqueous or salt-spray corrosion protocols
chosen.why: This approach tests the central mechanistic hypothesis—namely, that fine-tuned compositional variations in lightweight high-entropy alloys can stabilize beneficial short-range ordering that improves mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation behavior. By using direct property measurements on systematically doped versus baseline alloys, the study isolates the influence of composition on the hypothesized mechanism. This design leverages conventional, reliable testing procedures commonly used to evaluate aerospace and rail materials, providing a rigorous and definitive test of the proposed synergy.
